utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that my sixth channel is on. I don't know if it works. In any case, yesterday we discussed a number of instructors. I wanted to show you 1D5096, which is your document of March 1993. I'm sorry, 5096.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No. No translation, nothing in Serbian channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the usher could take a look into the microphone. Probably you need to turn up the volume after the change of the system. Do you hear me now, Mr. Karadzic? I hope it now has been sorted out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5096, please. I believe there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this document of yours?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I wrote it and sent it to the Drina Corps command and its department for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something briefly about this document, and we can see that you put the instructors under quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the Serbian version zoomed in. Thank you. Yes, that is correct. It is in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the document? What prompted you to write it? Did we indeed require some training but not of this sort, and did they abuse the principle of voluntariness, which was regulated by law, whereas, at the same time, they did as they pleased. Perhaps we can scroll down the document so you can remind yourself.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I am familiar with the contents. If you are interested in any details, I would have to read through it because I haven't seen it in a long time. In any case, it is my report sent to the Drina Corps command, its department for intelligence and security, where I stated all the problems concerning the stay of "instructors" from the FRY. As far as I remember, I listed all such problems that we had with them in Bratunac in general and in the Bratunac Brigade. Towards the end of the document, I believe I also offered my assessment as to what type of people they are and what their ultimate goal was. In addition to everything I have said thus far, I believe I also included information about what I knew of their engagement and who engaged them. I know precisely what it is all about, but if you want to go into specific details, I will be able to explain since I know exactly what was going on and what the problems were. I also know what it was that I informed my superior command about in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You agree that here you say that they were introduced to you and that they were supposed to carry out some training and withdraw from the municipality of Bratunac. They had no authority or right to meddle into any -- with any Bratunac affairs save for the training at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please scroll up so that I can follow it in the text. It seems you are following the text. Yes. This is what you just said. I said that I was told that they were being engaged to carry out specialist training following which they were to withdraw from the territory of Bratunac. This was acceptable to me, that kind of police and reconnaissance training was something we required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see the bottom half of the page. There you mentioned that a JPO unit was formed, a unit for special purposes, and by the end of the period it seems that they were no longer under anyone's control. Can you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For your benefit and the benefit of the Chamber, I need to establish -- I need to explain this establishment of the JPO unit. The way I was told initially was that they were there to carry out training. It was never foreseen that they should establish a unit of their own. It was planned that reconnaissance members of my brigade and members of the military police go to a facility, a camp, that was assigned to them where they were to attend training, specialist training in police work and reconnaissance work. However, the people I mentioned at the beginning of the letter who arrived established a unit. In keeping with the previous arrangement, we did send some policemen to their camp. We also sent members from the reconnaissance unit, but in addition to that personnel, they picked those from the Bratunac Brigade with whom we had problems, too, the most problematic soldiers, and included them in training. Instead of a training camp, we ended up with a very problematic, arrogant unit which no longer abided by what had been agreed. As I mention here, the unit called itself Special Purpose Unit. Yes, the establishment of a unit for "special purposes." They began mistreating people and intervene in the life of Bratunac according to their own beliefs. They had no respect for military rules, civilian authorities or the civilian police. They had their own rules which they imposed. In the text I go on to explain about what was going on and specify some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that in front of General Morillon they beat up the then commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and when you requested that the policemen sent to them for training be returned to their units, they turned on you, too; correct? It says: "They kicked Ognjenovic in the presence of General Morillon. When I requested that the policemen and reconnaissance personnel be returned, they turned on me as well." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they in conflict with Mauzer's unit at a certain point in time which, by that time, had resubordinated itself to the army? Did you know of their conflict and that Mauzer headed towards them with some cannons and APCs and then they released his men?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what happened, and I personally took part in resolving that situation. Some of Mauzer's soldiers were arrested by that unit which was not authorised to detain or bring in or interview anyone. It wasn't their task. Mauzer's unit, the Panthers from Bijeljina, was a very powerful unit ready for combat. They had both equipment and weapons as well as officers, and in terms of strength, they were far stronger than this unit. First, they tried to resolve it by peaceful means, asking that they return the soldiers they had arrested, and since they refused, Commander Mauzer and his officers ordered a movement towards their camp. They had APCs, combat vehicles, and they set out to attack them, to free their soldiers. We all intervened and eased the tension so as to avoid bloodshed, and in the end they indeed released those soldiers from the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to the bottom of the page. There you say: "In the brigade in Bratunac, there is great dissatisfaction, and it is only a matter of moment when there would be an armed clash between them, the citizens, and the officers and soldiers of the brigade." It means that the citizens were against them, too; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, everyone in Bratunac was against them, starting with the citizens, members of the police, civilian authorities, and members of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seemed they had a special taste for SDS people. They mistreated them in particular, including Deronjic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mistreated everyone including Deronjic, who was the then Municipal Board President in Bratunac. They mistreated the municipal president. They attacked the police station. There was an exchange of fire. And as you can see in my report, there were also individual examples of mistreatment of members of the Bratunac Brigade, detention, beatings of officers who passed out due to such beatings. And when my officer, assistant commander for logistics, was arrested and after I saw what they had done to him, I turned to Mijovic, who was their commander, and I told him that unless he released Trisic and stopped mistreating members of the Bratunac Brigade, I was prepared to come there with the units and liquidate them all to get my soldiers, reconnaissance men, and policemen back. And then they were free to train whoever they wanted. After that threat, he indeed put a stop to it. I told him that I would report it to my superior command, as I did. I explained all of the problems that existed and asked that they be withdrawn from our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the middle of the page you say that they seemed to have occupied some check-points, took upon themselves to carry out police duties and even looted UNPROFOR and UNHCR convoys and that it, too, contributed to the overall situation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I wrote here and everything you read out now is correct. They tried -- actually, it wasn't they tried. At one point in time they absolutely took over Bratunac, life in general in Bratunac. And the saddest of all was the fact that no one dared confront them or oppose them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that this was before the liberation of Podrinje and that Bratunac as such was isolated except vis-a-vis Serbia, that you could not reach Pale through our own territory? You would have to go out to Serbia and then take hundreds of kilometres, taking the roundabout way, Zvornik, Caparde, Sekovic, and only then could you get to Pale. You wrote this on the 5th of March and the liberation of Podrinje took place sometime towards the end of March, beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this in March, and it is correct that the winter/spring offensive was over by then, end of March, beginning of April, and we did not have any communication. That's what you asked me about. We did not have any communication through Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, Vlasenica and Pale. We had to go through Serbia and then to Zvornik on the Bosnian side and then further on towards Sekovici, Vlasenica, that area up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not taking the main road via Konjevic Polje but different byroads; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, different byroads.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2062, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you whether you agree that at that point in time, the Muslim side had under their control a large part of the territory from Zepa, Srebrenica, parts of the Bratunac and Milici municipalities and Zvornik, all the way up to Kamenica. So this is a rather big area that they linked up, and they kept it under their control until we launched our spring offensive.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you an affirmative answer with respect to all of these territories that you referred to. As for the territory of my municipality where I was involved, I can tell even more specifically that in this period before the winter/spring offensive, that is to say, until the attack on Kravica, when it was taken on the 7th of January, 1993, the forces of the Muslim 28th Division kept all of the territory of Bratunac under their control. The only part that remained free was part of the urban area, say 4 or 5 kilometres from town maximum. All the other villages had fallen and were under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in many of the peace plans it had been envisaged that large parts of Podrinje would be part of the Muslim republic, the Muslim constituent republic, and that this struggle of theirs was completely unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot draw any conclusions as to what they find necessary or unnecessary. If I understand you correctly, you're speaking about the Muslims. Of course, I know of the Muslim objective of having Podrinje within their republic. Now, whether they needed to fight or not, that is really something that was for them to decide, and I cannot comment upon that, and I do not wish to comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the following: At that time -- actually, is it correct, then, that in Zepa, Konjevic Polje, Srebrenica, all the way up to Zvornik, Oric's soldiers could have been in that entire area, and indeed they were there when necessary?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Srebrenica, I think it is indispensable to say that, first of all, they were the armed forces of Srebrenica, and then they established the 28th Division. And after that, they brought together all their forces in the area, including Zepa, and this became the 8th Operative Group. The forces of the 8th Operative or Operations Group were in the entire area that you referred to. And this 8th Operations Group that covered this broader area that you referred to consisted of forces from Srebrenica, that is to say, the municipality of Srebrenica, the municipality of Zepa, and the areas that belonged to the Bratunac municipality, and these were the units that were in Konjevic Polje and Cerska. So all of these forces were covering the area that you mentioned, and they were all within the 8th Operations Group under the command of Commander Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember their actions at the time aimed against neighbouring Serb villages, and do you remember that they were very active in combat upon orders from their Main Staff? For example, incursions like the one in Kravica on Christmas Day in 1993, and elsewhere. So, please, could you tell us about the end of 1992, December, when Skelani fell victim. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that, about the degree of suffering at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know exactly about the period when I was in Bratunac, and the period that you are referring to is primarily the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993. I just wish to correct you on one point. You said "incursion in Kravica." The attack against Kravica was a large-scale Muslim offensive involving a large number of Muslim soldiers who were attacking Kravica from all sides. For the 28th Division, this was a strategic goal in Podrinje, to take Kravica and Podrinje and place the area under their control. That is indeed what happened. Everything that you're interested in in relation to attacks against villages in my municipality and the area of responsibility of my brigade, that is to say, from the attack against Bjelovac -- actually, first Sase and then Bjelovac and then Kravica, these large-scale attacks and offensives are something that I can talk about. But, in a single sentence, a large number, say, percentage-wise, 92 or 93 per cent of the territory of Bratunac was under the control of the Muslim forces until the winter/spring offensive. So it was only 4 or 5 kilometres within Bratunac that had remained, and this offensive that was launched by the Muslims was so fierce that even the town of Bratunac itself was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to Kravica, Bjelovac and other places just like Skelani, Fakovici, are infamous because of the slaughter of civilians, when many women and children were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During all of these attacks, Skelani, Fakovici, Bjelovac, Sase, Kravica, there were military casualties, but there were also a great many civilian casualties. It's really been a very long time, almost 20 years, 17, 18 years, whatever. I no longer remember the structure of the casualties of all these attacks, but in my office I did have specific information as to how many soldiers were killed during these attacks and how many civilians were killed. What I can state here with certainty is that there were soldiers who had been killed but also that there were a great many massacred civilians that had nothing to do with the military, women, children, young girls, old men over 70 and 80 years old and so on. I do not have an exact list of names, but the Institute for War Crimes headed by Ivanisevic has this information, because I gave this to them after every operation and every massacre that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me refresh your memory a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5097. Could we take a look at that, please. The date is the 9th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that point in time the chief of security was Ranko Kuljanin in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that at that point in time Ranko Kuljanin was chief of security, and I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We don't have the translation yet, but I would like to ask you to take a look at this document and to present it to us. This is a report on the examination of an imprisoned Muslim, and he's talking about a planned attack from Srebrenica and Glogova, and he says where it would start from, from Petokrake, that hill up there, isn't it? So Oric would command that attack from Petokrake and so on. Could I please ask you to read this and present this document to the Trial Chamber in two or three sentences.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do give me a bit of time, because this is the first time I see this report. Could I just briefly take a look at it. Yes. I have seen the content of this intelligence report. Could -- yes. Yes. That's right. I would like to see the upper part. The 9th of January, if I can see this right, 1993, is the date. Please, what was the question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that what was discovered here was that there was an attack against Bratunac that was being planned from the area of Srebrenica and an Intervention Platoon came to the area of Bratunac for sabotage purposes, and that they found mortar shells for an 82-millimetre mortar in Sase and so on. So you did find out that the attack would take place within two or three days; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the period after the fall of Kravica. Kravica was attacked on the 7th and it fell on the 7th, and by the 9th of January, 1993, it had completely been taken. All other territories -- well, this is precisely the situation I talked about a moment ago. Everything had been taken except for 4 or 5 kilometres within Bratunac itself. Glogova, Kravica, Muslim forces had entered all of that. That is 4 or 5 kilometres away from the centre of town itself. From the area of Potocari, the forces were in the area of Budak, and that is also 4 kilometres away from Bratunac, from the town of Bratunac, from the centre of town. From the area of Fakovici, from that direction. The Muslim forces were in Voljavica or, rather, at the boundary at Pobrdje, and that is only 2 or 3 kilometres away from the town of Bratunac. So it is only this one part along the Drina River, that is to say, along the old road that goes to Zvornik, it was only that part that hadn't been attacked, say, until this day, this particular day, the 9th. And then the village of Polom was attacked. That is this area by the Drina River. And the Muslims took that area, Gornji Polom, and they almost got to the Drina River itself in that part. So this entire area had fallen, and they took up very favourable positions for taking the town itself. Without even reading this report, this intelligence report, I can say that my information was also that an attack against Bratunac was being prepared and that it was hardly likely that Bratunac would be able to defend itself in view of the general collapse of the units that were in the area of Kravica. People got killed. Those who did not get killed fled to Serbia across the Drina, and then other people fled to Serbia too. So we had very few forces. We took up new positions because we had been moved from our old positions as they were taken by the Muslim forces, and the fall of Bratunac was expected then, in 1993, in this period that I see referred to in this report, that is to say, sometime in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the same time you have problems with different instructors. Well, in all fairness, somewhat later, if we remember that text, but they were already in Bratunac, or they took advantage of this dangerous situation, and they offered their services. Do you know when it was that they actually came?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the exact date when they came, but they had already established this camp of theirs, and I think that they were in Bratunac, but I really cannot say what the exact date is when they arrived, because I no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Concerning this document of yours that the authorities managed to get rid of them and was the army able to do the same? Were they driven out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following my report, they stayed in Bratunac for a while until the organs of the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff negotiated, so to say, their withdrawal. Irrespective of what I wrote and what I asked for, for their withdrawal it is either required to use force or that they be made to withdraw by the person who sent them there in the first place. They were directly answerable to Colonel Ilic who was in the operations and training sector of the Main Staff. My information was that he was their boss and that he brought them there. They had been in Skelani previously, as he had been. So it was a connection from some earlier periods, and he held sway over them. He had influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He, too, was dismissed later on; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, because of different crimes and participation in plunder together with this unit, but I'm not familiar with any details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this document, and it could be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2063, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us try and see what the situation was before our offensive, but as I call it, counter-offensive, in the spring of 1993. Do we agree that the area where the 8th Operations Group was, commanded by Naser Oric, kept bothering, so to say, the Serb units and settlements along the separation line? They were in constant activity and things simply became unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know for a fact is that until the counter-offensive of the Serb forces was launched, we had lost many men, assets, and equipment as well as territory. That is evident. Of course, it was war booty for the forces of the 28th Division. That is why we conclude that there was intensive combat. The Muslims were attacking, and we were then defending ourselves and withdrawing as we did. We kept losing territory day by day, and we were reduced to the territory I have already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We agree, don't we, that the main road from Vlasenica and Milici to Zvornik was mostly under their control, and we couldn't use it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood well, you said the road from Vlasenica to Konjevic Polje and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And up to Zvornik. It is the best road, the main road, to Zvornik and Serbia from Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of my brigade, the part of the road which forks -- after the fork in Konjevic Polje was the most important for my unit. We couldn't use it from Konjevic Polje to Zvornik, and the road from Konjevic Polje to Bratunac and on to Serbia, from Konjevic Polje all the way up to Hranca and Donji Magasici which is 4 kilometres from Bratunac, that part was controlled by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that our only way of communicating by road with Zvornik, Bijeljina, and Banja Luka was to use a side road from Vlasenica to Tisca, Sekovici, Caparde and Crni Vrh? It is a byroad which is much longer.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of that road and I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information that that route was frequently attacked, too, and that the Muslim forces ambushed not only military units but civilian vehicles, buses, and that a great number of civilian passengers were killed or injured there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not within the area of responsibility of my brigade. I would rather not go into things I am not certain of. I don't know such ambushes there because I never worked on such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Our counter-offensive was launched, which was quite successful and resulted in the liberation of one part of Podrinje up to Srebrenica itself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the winter and spring offensive, all the territory we had lost previously was returned, including the liberation of Konjevic Polje and Cerska, as well as the liberation of all the territory that had previously been captured by Muslim forces, including the road I mentioned, which was important for us to travel between my unit and our superior commands, between Bratunac, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Vlasenica, Pale, and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the Muslim offensives, what was happening with our civilian population in the villages which fell into their hands? Some of them were -- some of the people were killed. What about those who were still alive? Did they flee or did they remain in the territory controlled by the other side?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the Muslim offensive -- offensives, when those villages were occupied, like Skelani, Fakovici, Kravica, et cetera, which were occupied in their biggest attacks, once that territory was occupied, the civilians for the most part withdrew to Bratunac. No one remained in that area. A great percentage of those civilians then went on across the Drina to Serbia to stay with their families and relatives or friends. That is where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that they killed even the cattle in those villages and set fire to the houses so that the inhabitants were unable to return even if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm a part of your question which has to do with looting and burning of houses and property, including outhouses and all such buildings. I could see for myself that in every village that was entered by the Muslim forces, after they had plundered, they set them ablaze. There were killed cattle, but I can't confirm that they killed all cattle. They would come and take the cattle away following village occupations. I just wanted to explain something else for the benefit of the Chamber. With every such attack and entry into the village that was being attacked, the army came in first and carried out the combat part of the operation. Following the soldiers, practically immediately or shortly thereafter, a great many civilians arrived. I would dare say that there were thousands of civilians who entered those villages. I could see that for myself in Bjelovac and in Kravica. After the soldiers had completed the combat part, the civilians came in and took away everything they could find in the village, food, corn, wheat, furniture, other things, as well as livestock, sheep, cattle, et cetera, and only then they torched the whole place down. In Kravica not a single house was spared as well as in Bjelovac and Fakovici. That was their modus operandi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that their civilians left Kamenica and Cerska even before our army arrived and they gathered in Konjevic Polje and went on to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This detail that you are referring to, to the effect that they assembled before we entered Cerska and Konjevic Polje, that is something I am not aware of it. But I do know this: It was a very powerful attack on Konjevic Polje and Cerska which was executed by our forces. I know about that, and I know that all civilians from those villages withdrew before our units entered the villages. That attack was not aimed at Cerska on a single day, but the attack included the area from Zvornik to Konjevic Polje, which is some 30 or 35 kilometres from Cerska. As the Serb forces advanced, the civilians realised they were in danger and withdrew before the advancing forces. I cannot say whether they all withdrew or whether someone remained or was captured, any of the civilians, but I do know that in general they were withdrawing to Srebrenica, which was controlled by the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, can you assist, and I stress assist, the Chamber with the relevance of this line of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be happy to, Your Excellency. Mr. Nikolic, during our interview, when we discussed what preceded the key events he testified to, he said that there were enormous hatred not only as a result of this war but also from World War II and all the previous wars. I was simply trying to paint that picture so that we can see what made the July of 1995 situation possible. What was the basis, the cause for action of individuals, groups, and perhaps even commands. Not in order to justify but to understand how things developed up to the point that the events we are, in particular, interested in could take place, and besides the issue of Cerska was supposed to go in that direction, as well as the instance when I put a stop to the operation in 1993, and Mr. Nikolic, as an army officer, will be able to answer those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you very much indeed. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, time is limited. Speaking for myself, I'm struggling to understand why you need two hours and a half to try to simply show -- to paint the picture. Please continue. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Your Honours, no objection, sorry to interrupt, but in Mr. Karadzic's explanation to Your Honour Judge Baird, just to be clear, Mr. Nikolic in the interview where I was present by video-link did discuss that there was enormous hatred in the area which has built up, but the basis, the cause for action of individual groups and perhaps even commands, that's something Dr. Karadzic is saying, I assume, is relevant, but it's not something Mr. Nikolic said in the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will try to go over this topic more quickly, Mr. Nikolic. Do you recall that following the liberation of Cerska, in the media and public there was an entire campaign of lies where it was stated that there was bloodshed there and massacres, and General Morillon came for that very reason to the area seeking to verify that for himself? Do you recall such stories?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to Cerska, and I don't know much about it. As for this specific question, I know that in the media there was much talk of Cerska, and there was a lot of negative reporting about what had happened there. I don't recall a specific date, but around that time of the attack on Cerska and the offensive I do remember that General Morillon went there personally, but that's the extent of information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also remember that in the foreign media and in the local media it was said that the Serbian forces, the VRS entered Srebrenica in 1993, and a massacre was perpetrated there, and there were streams of blood. They were barely able to show that this was false. Do you remember this at the time that it had been declared that Srebrenica had fallen?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there being information conveyed according to which Srebrenica had fallen and according to which the Serbian forces had entered the town, but I don't remember information according to which a massacre had been perpetrated and that there had been a bloodshed. I know about this fabrication. The information was erroneously presented. The Serbian forces were in the vicinity of Srebrenica and around Srebrenica but not in Srebrenica. I apologise. In fact, I really do not remember the details with regard to those fabrications, those manipulations. In general terms I know about the sort of information provided, but I wasn't concerned with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Tolimir case -- in the Tolimir case, page 12544, you said that you had almost taken Srebrenica but that your forces were stopped by an order from the Main Staff and the president of the republic. Could we see P43, please, so that you can have a look at that document that you probably had in mind when you stated this in the Tolimir case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P0043. D0043, D. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at this. It's dated the 16th of April; is that correct? Is this the order that you were referring to halt all VRS activity against Srebrenica and in its surroundings except for those necessary for defence. Please have a look at the text, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just need a little time because this is the first time I've seen this document. Yes, I've read through this order of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's a document that put an end to our operation that could quite easily have resulted in the taking of Srebrenica. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on Srebrenica -- or, rather, ceasing to proceed with the operation meant that our forces were prevented from entering the town. I personally participated in that operation with my unit. I was in the Pribicevac sector, in the Crni -- Crni Vugara [as interpreted] sector, and in the course of that operation, a day, one and a half days or two days were needed at the most to enter Srebrenica but three or four hours would have been sufficient, in fact, to actually enter the town because it was as if there were barely any more resistance from the Muslim armed forces. The order you have shown me is an order I see for the first time now, and when I was answering Mr. Tolimir's questions, I didn't have this order in mind. Today is the first time I've seen this document. In Pribicevac there was a -- there was a communication system and via that system we were informed in the evening hours at the time of the attack, I don't know the exact date. Perhaps it was on the 15th of April or perhaps on the 14th of April. I don't know exactly when we went to that sector, but in any event, in the evening hours, it was the eve of the day on which we had planned to enter Srebrenica, and at that time we received an oral order according to which the commander of the Main Staff and the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Ratko Mladic, had ordered the Serbian forces not to enter Srebrenica and to stay at their positions. This was the order that was conveyed to the units. I don't know whether it was conveyed to all the units, but the unit in which I was, on the axis I was on, received that order. Given that no one launched an attack on the following day, I assumed that all the other forces around Srebrenica involved in the attack also received that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at item 5. Is it correct that it wasn't requested that soldiers be transformed into POWs but into civilians? In item 6, it says: "Don't conduct any investigation into war crimes ..." I, in fact, prohibited the conduct of investigations into their war crimes until the situation calmed down.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think it's necessary for me to comment on this order of yours. It's quite clear. Your positions, you orders with regard to certain issues is quite clear, but as I have said, I've never seen this order before, and I don't think it makes sense for me to comment on it. I've told you what I know in relation to your order and in relation to halting the attack, but it is true. I can confirm this, that at that period of time there was not even the possibility of proceeding. We didn't even enter Srebrenica. We didn't have any prisoners and so on and so forth. What you have written down here, well, this is your order, and I don't think I should comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's quite sufficient. Are you confirming that you didn't take prisoners then and that there were no investigations, their soldiers, well, it was sufficient for them to hand over their weapons to UNPROFOR and to be treated as civilians. No one was requesting that they surrender.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that, that I knew that at the time, but -- because when we received the order I didn't know the contents of the order, so I can't confirm that. What I can confirm is that in my brigade's area of responsibility, my brigade and I myself didn't have POWs, nor did we have any tasks or the possibility to check the situation with regard to disarmament, surrendering weapons, and so on and so forth. These are things that you regulated through your order, but I wasn't aware of this, and I didn't participate in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any information according to which the military circles held it against me because this operation to take Srebrenica was halted? Did many officers and soldiers hold this against me? Was this an unpopular move in the eyes of the military from the point of view of military and defence interests?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is about the situation in my brigade, my unit. There was dissatisfaction because of that order. All the soldiers and officers were very unhappy, because the operation had been halted and because you had issued such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that afterwards, Srebrenica was declared a protected zone, and it was supposed to be a protected zone for the civilians without any troops present in it. It was supposed to be a demilitarised zone.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately afterwards, immediately after the ban on VRS units entering Srebrenica, General Morillon and UN forces arrived. And as far as I know, on the 18th of April, Srebrenica was declared to be a demilitarised and protected zone under the protection of UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it never was demilitarised. The military continued to strengthen its forces in relation to its structure and the weapons it disposed of. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the information I have, from that point in time up until the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, Srebrenica was not demilitarised. It was not disarmed, and the military developed. There was the formation of the 8th Operations Group which raised their level of organisation to a higher level with regard to 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we move on to next topic, could we collapse the English and zoom in B/C/S part, in particular the signature part. Since it was not translated, Mr. Nikolic, would you kindly read what is in the stamp, a round stamp. The upper part seems to be Republika Srpska, but ... We can zoom in a bit once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't decipher this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I help? Does it say the "President of the Republic"? Is that in the lower part of the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is what I see, and I can't see it. You can enlarge this as much as you like, but I can't decipher this down here. I can see P, R, E, only three letters, and I can't read anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the top to see the heading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, that's sufficient. Shall we see the stamp again, the signature part again. I am not sure if you can answer this question, but I take it because you -- it is your native language. You see there "Dr. Radovan Karadzic" in Cyrillic. Do you usually put a dot after "Dr."?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know. I don't want to speculate. I don't think you do put a dot. That's what I think, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at 1D5104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But while this is still on the screen, Mr. Nikolic, would you agree that this was written on a typewriter, not on a computer, this order? Can you have a look at this order again? Can you see that a typewriter was used and not a computer?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make assumptions, but please don't put such questions to me, because I don't want to guess. I don't know whether a typewriter was used or not. I don't know what the difference would be if it had been written on a computer. I don't know what was used to write this order, and I don't want to -- to guess, so please don't put such questions to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D5104. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 1st of January, 1994. Please look at it carefully. In the spring of 1993, it was declared to be a protected zone, and this is what the Main Staff of the supreme commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina orders on the 1st of January. It was prepared a little earlier perhaps. Here's the order. Is it true that the 8th Operations Group is being formed, the 8th Srebrenica Operations Group? Have a look at the structure on the first page. It mentions the 280th, the 281st Brigade being established. Does this relate to the strengthening of the army after the zone had been declared to be a protected zone? If it's easier for you, perhaps the usher could give you a hard copy, whereas all the other participants could look at the screen, at the English version.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a problem. I can see everything quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you're ready, ask for us to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, five brigades up to the 284th and Independent Mountain Battalion. Was all this carried out? All the orders here, were they carried out?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether everything ordered here was carried out, that's not a question for me. I can't answer that question. As to whether I have any information about the reorganisation of their armed forces in Srebrenica, yes, I did have information on the transformation of the 28th Division, on the establishment of the 8th Operations Group, which included within that group all the forces from the area of Srebrenica and a brigade from Zepa. And naturally, I also had information about the establishment of these units that had been listed here, from the 280th Brigade up to the independent units and the headquarters support units that were formed as part of the 8th Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a look at the next page in the English version and please have a look at item 1, mobilisation preparations. Here they're asking 110th per cent of unit strength and of equipment and materiel. Does this mean that the unit has to be fully equipped as per wartime establishment and even more equipped than necessary when manpower is in question? And it says the Secretariat for National Defence should supervise these additional -- this additional manpower. So they didn't have a problem with manpower; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You told me to take a look at mobilisation preparations, that section. It's quite obvious that the brigades and other units that are referred to in the previous text were supposed to be manned 100 per cent on the basis of the mobilisation plan, or, rather, 110 per cent. So that means that these units were supposed to be established and fully manned and equipped with materiel in accordance with this written information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that word, they were not handicapped, and they were not supposed to be diminished in any way; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I see in front of me, they were manned 100 per cent. That is to say that they were not supposed to be decreased or restricted in terms of manpower or materiel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the last page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your brigade took part of this upon itself; right? They had to work vis-a-vis the separation line and the area of responsibility of your brigade probably matched the boundaries of the municipality itself; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to correct you a bit so that all of this would be correct. The area of responsibility of my brigade did not correspond to the area of the municipality. It did take part of the municipality of Srebrenica as well. However, you are right. Whenever possible, the area of responsibility would coincide with the territory of the municipality involved. I can confirm here that -- actually, I saw the map a few days ago, and I measured the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade. It was between 42 and 45 kilometres. That's the area of responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade, including the 4th Battalion from the Zvornik Brigade in this period, the critical period. So the area was between 42 and 45 kilometres, facing the enclave of Srebrenica. It was controlled by -- or, rather, members of my brigade held that part of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in spite of the demilitarisation agreement and the protection of Srebrenica, Srebrenica did engage some of our brigades, and can you tell us which brigades of ours had to be there? You know about your own brigade, 40-something kilometres of front line there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around Srebrenica, that is to say, around the protected enclave, I mean, I'm talking about the period after the 18th of April. So in addition to my brigade, on the right wing facing Srebrenica there was the Milici Brigade. There was also a Light Infantry Brigade practically identical in terms of its personnel level when compared to the Bratunac Brigade. And in the area of Pribicevac, Zeleni Jadar, et cetera, on the left, that is, was the Independent Skelani Battalion. That was the situation in the period that we're discussing now. Just by way of information, I'd like to add that from time to time we had parts of other units, from other brigades and corps. Roughly, there would always be one battalion, sometimes perhaps a Police Battalion of Republika Srpska, that would also be at these positions. Sometimes battalions from other brigades, corps, et cetera. However, the permanent composition was the Independent Battalion of Skelani, the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, and the Milici Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And these reinforcements were never brought in for offensive purposes but only with a view to consolidating the defence of Serb areas until July 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that basically they were brought in to reinforce our positions. The continued permanent task was to separate the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. Usually when this was insisted upon, additional forces were required to keep these positions, these spaces in between that were not covered, so that this can be done in proper military fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the break, we are going to show that document, how they used this for illegal purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2064, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Registrar is kindly requested to repeat the number loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D2064. Yes. We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned today that these reinforcements were there exclusively for Defence purposes and also to break up the link between Zepa and Srebrenica. Do we agree that this territorial link between them was not legitimate and was not in accordance with the agreement on protected areas, and the road that would link the two enclaves and Skelani was supposed to be in our territory and that they linked up the two enclaves in contravention of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be very specific. I never saw the agreement in writing, and I do not know all the things that are defined in the agreement, and I cannot give you an answer to that question. I cannot answer you in the affirmative, whether that's what it says there, that there should be no communication whatsoever. What I know for sure is that we tried to prevent this communication between the two enclaves, and my understanding of this was that this intention of ours was fully legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Zepa was a more favourable location for bringing in weapons illegally by helicopter and that there was also more food in Zepa, and that on a daily basis, caravans of 50 horses went from Zepa to Srebrenica and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we just have a time-frame for when caravans of 50 horses daily went from Zepa to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the time before the fall of Srebrenica and Zepa, that is to say, between the -- in the period from the declaration of the protected zone until 1995. So the witness already did testify about this. Perhaps it would be best for him to tell us in which periods this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to answer the first question you put, and that had to do with Zepa and your question whether the situation was better there and whether conditions were more favourable for receiving supplies. I don't know what the situation in Zepa was, and I do not wish to go into that at all. I do not wish to answer that type of question, because I really do not know what the situation was like there. I do know that in the area of Zepa - that is what I know for sure, that is - that in Veliko Polje, Malo Polje and in the area of Zepa, there was an area that was very convenient for the landing of helicopters and for bringing whatever could be brought in by helicopter. I know with certainty -- so I know with certainty that between Zepa and Srebrenica there was communication that was almost permanent and that there was communication involving trips to Zepa from Srebrenica and vice versa. Regardless to the extent to which the Serb army wanted to separate them, the configuration of the terrain is such that you simply could not prevent that kind of communication, on foot, through those caravans, as you call them. That was there all the time. Throughout the war, that is. All this time from the beginning of the war, when Srebrenica and Zepa were declared demilitarised zones and all the way up until the fall of both enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about that, did you not, in your interview with the NIOD institute on the 20th of October, 2000, on page 5. 1D5056. We can take a look at this. 1D5056, on page 5. What you say there is that up to 50 horses went there and back every day. Do we agree that there were weapons there and ammunition and other goods? Can this be zoomed in and then page 5. Do you remember this interview, giving this interview to this institute?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And my answer to your question is that that is correct. Actually, that is what I know, namely, that this transport -- or everything, different kinds of goods that are necessary for normal life, and then ammunition, weapons, everything that they exchanged by way of these contacts. Well, those are the questions I spoke about. As for their movements, trade, supplies, and mutual contacts, I had information about all of that and I have testified about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that in July 1995, too, such a task was underway and that it began at the Echo Observation Post -- or, rather, in the Zeleni Jadar area, which means in the area between -- that links up these two enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, I believe that the direct cause for the attack at the control, at the check-point, and the attempt to take up the enclave in the area of Zeleni Jadar, there the trigger for that attack was not to prevent -- or, rather, it wasn't the only trigger for the attack. One of the reasons why the VRS did that was that the Drina Corps command and the Main Staff demanded, requested, that the Zeleni Jadar check-point be moved some 400 to 500 metres towards Srebrenica to be within the enclave, because the Serb side considered throughout this time that their check-point was actually without the borders, outside of the borders of the enclave and that it should be pushed back into the enclave. And the other reason was that this check-point, by the very fact of where it was, actually hampered the Serb side to provide supplies for its rear, and the position of this check-point also hindered the communication between Zeleni towards Milici, Jasenovi and in that general direction. In other words, that check-point was smack in the middle of that intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this period of time when Srebrenica was a protected area, did you have information, perhaps not precise, on the number of people living in Srebrenica, on the population in Srebrenica? In other words, do you know that they actually presented -- exaggerated the numbers of inhabitants when they presented them to the international sources in order to get more humanitarian aid than they would normally have gotten? In order to give it to the army.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I won't pretend that I had precise information, but I do have general assessments and -- on the number of civilians and the population in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like now to show you a document of theirs from January 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 4372 from the 65 ter list, please. 4372. Could we just zoom in on this document, please. We are expecting to have the interpretation as well -- the translation but I will read it out for you. This is Bosnia-Herzegovina, Srebrenica municipality. The date is 11 January 1994, and it is sent to the statistics bureau of the BH republic, the Department of Statistics in Tuzla and the district secretary for defence in Tuzla. And then it says: "Pursuant to your document 031-01/93 of 7 January 1994, we forward the requested information as follows: "The number of the local inhabitants in the municipality is 9.791. "The local population which was dislocated within the municipality numbers 10.756. "The number of expelled people from other municipalities is 16.708. "Note: The information you requested are forwarded for your statistics, which you should not provide to international organisations because in our communications with them, we used the figure of 45.000 inhabitants."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this consistent with what you knew about the situation in early 1994, the number of people there, as well as this exaggerated figure that is presented?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my assessment -- and of course, I did not look at the structure the way it was presented here by the Muslim authorities. My assessment had to do with the total number of the Muslim population, and I can tell you that my assessment was similar to the ones we see here, and in my assessments I always had the figure of between 40.000 and 45.000. These were my assessments, but now I see here that there are some -- there's some precise information for the statistics bureau. So what I can say is that my assessment was similar to what we see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know this person, Fahrudin Salihovic, the president of the Srebrenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had several conversations with representatives of the civilian authorities and the Muslim army in Potocari after the zones were declared demilitarised. Whether Salihovic was at the time the president -- I think that I did not have contacts with the president. I think I had contacts with the chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we add up these figures, we'll see that the total would be around 37.000, whereas what they're presenting is 45.000, which means that it's a figure inflated by some 8.000, based on this more precise information. In other words, there were 24.000 local people, and as for refugees, about 16.000 in total. Let me see what that comes out to. So we get the figure of some 36.000 to 37.000; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When you add it all up, that's approximately the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can we agree that this was the peak and that later on, in view of the legal and illegal departures, the number could only have gone down in July 1995. It couldn't have gone up.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of this overall assessment, I can say that I had different assessments at different times, so generally speaking, I cannot really claim, as I sit here, that this was the maximum figure. I performed these assessments on a continuous basis at the time. The figures, the numbers were larger at times, at times they were smaller, but in my assessment, the largest concentration in Srebrenica was after the spring -- winter and spring offensive, in other words, when from Konjevic Polje and Cerska and that area, Glogova and all the other villages, people started coming in after the VRS took control there. And approximately I would say that I at times even arrived at a larger figure than I see here, but I do have to believe the official statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But can we agree that there were departures, but there was no mass influx at the time following this date that we see here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I see Mr. Nicholls is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer, Mr. Nikolic. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, just Mr. Reid's found a translation and can upload it for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not challenging the authenticity of this document, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know yet, Your Honour. I have to look at it a bit more carefully, but we do have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the translation? Is it uploaded? Yes. What is your submission as to the admissibility of this document, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2065, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you just answer this question. Is it correct that as of January 1st, for instance, 1994, up until July 1995, there were no people who were fleeing into Srebrenica, and, rather, that people were leaving out of Srebrenica, so that this figure, if we compare it to the figure we saw a moment ago, in July 1995, could only have been smaller, not larger?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, after Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone, there was no reason anymore for mass influxes of population into Srebrenica. Yes, there were individuals who came from Zepa and other areas, but there was no mass influx. As far as I know for certain is that sometime in 1994, I can't tell you the exact date, but sometime in early 1994, with approval and in an organised manner and according to plan, people from the enclave left for Kladanj and Tuzla and other areas, and they numbered around 3.500 to 4.000 people. They left in organised convoys and with the approval of the VRS and the authorities that were competent in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But there were also able-bodied men who fled, crossing over our territory. Did you know of that? And they would organise chases after these deserters.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the information and what I know with certainty is that there were individual flights from Srebrenica, but there were also individual arrivals from Tuzla -- of people from Tuzla into Srebrenica. But if we are talking about a mass exodus, then we can only refer to the convoy that I spoke about a moment ago. But these individual arrivals could not really affect in any significant way the total number of people in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see 1D5079. Unfortunately, we don't have a translation, so I will not refer to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you -- I'd like to go back to some other matters. You had information about the inflow of humanitarian aid to the Srebrenica enclave. Can we agree that these convoys were first checked when they entered Republika Srpska at the Karakaj and Zepa bridge, and the second, the next check, was at the Yellow Bridge on the way out of Republika Srpska, between Bratunac and Srebrenica, and that you were in charge of this stretch of the road.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can agree in principle, but I would like to be specific and quite clear. We are talking about detailed checks here. If that's what you're referring to, then I can agree with that. So the first detailed check of any convoys that entered Republika Srpska was done at the first crossing once they entered the territory. Now, each convoy leaving Srebrenica and every individual departure of any representatives of international organisations from there were checked at the Yellow Bridge because that was the first check-point when leaving the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that they inflated the number of inhabitants by 8.000, in view of the fact that a large number of that population lived in villages and that they lived on their own land, so they had cattle and they also produced food, do you feel that or do you think that a large portion of that humanitarian aid actually went to the 28th Division, and had it not been so, that the population would have had quantities of food that were sufficient for them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, bear in your mind that you are not giving evidence. I don't think the witness has confirmed the number 8.000 in terms of inflation. Yes, Mr. Nikolic. Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer the last question. It does not pose a problem. But I also wanted to say that I discussed my assessment, and I confirmed only the figure I worked with. Everything else Mr. Karadzic said comes from the document he has shown, and I can neither confirm nor deny. That figure has to do with elections. The other part of the question put by Mr. Karadzic is something I can clearly answer. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an explanation which may be useful for the Chamber. Yesterday, we discussed the structure of the armed forces in Srebrenica, and we discussed the principles of how those units were manned. Almost 100 per cent of the personnel were municipal residents, people who lived there or arrived from other parts of the country which they had abandoned when their homes were attacked by the Serb forces. The exact situation was on the Serb side as well. My unit relied exclusively on the local inhabitants. Even if one wanted to, the army could not be separated or cut off from the population. Every soldier in the enclave was somebody's brother or father with a family there. So you can't split two and say, This is the aid for the civilians and the soldiers will not use it. They will, whether you want it or not, because they are members of the families. Now, as for how much was taken up by the army of that total aid or how much it kept only for themselves, that is only something I can assess. In any case, the quantities entering Srebrenica, in my assessment, based on the number of people that were supposed to receive it, in my view, the quantities were insufficient. I don't know whether I was correct in presuming that, but I shared my assessments with you. I believed that given the number of the population, the humanitarian aid that was arriving was insufficient for a normal life. On the other hand, I agree that this humanitarian aid which arrived was to a large extent used by members of the 28th Division -- or, rather, members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps it's a call for speculation, but it is a fact that those five brigades were only the users of food rather than producers, and that was another aggravating factor. If the enclave had indeed been demilitarised, perhaps the situation would have been different. Otherwise, we had soldiers who had no other duties and consumed that aid. If it is too complicated, I will withdraw this question. But the fact remains that the soldiers were there to fight. They were not there to produce food as they should have. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Mr. Nikolic. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one, it was a statement not a question in any fair sense. I think Mr. Karadzic realised that at the end and that's why he started to withdraw it. And second, it's the -- the false premise built in, unless he has a basis for it, that had everybody -- had these men -- with the amount of people in the enclave, that there would have been plenty of food for everybody if everybody had been farming. That's just, I think, not in evidence and is a misstatement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I note he has withdrawn. Let us continue. Mr. Nikolic, can you answer the question? Shall I repeat it for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be so kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you put your last question yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the fact that it was supposed to have been a demilitarised zone, were the able-bodied men deployed to the brigades rather than being at home? They should have been there and not at the front lines. In other words, by virtue of their deployment, they became a nonproductive category of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you not put just one question at a time, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In a year or two I'll be more skilled in this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer this question, Your Honour. I have understood. I can answer it precisely. Yes, we fully agree that the members of the 28th Division and of other units in Srebrenica were armed and that Srebrenica was not a demilitarised zone. Their basic task was engagement in the units where they were deployed. I absolutely agree. As for the second part, we can only make a premise based on the previous conclusion. In other words, they were engaged in one task and were unable to work on anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 1D5075. Translation is still pending, but since it's a relatively short document I would kindly ask for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, 1994, Oric reported on some negotiations with the aggressor side, i.e., the Serbs. He says that demilitarisation lines were being discussed and the issue of fire being opened on the population inside the demilitarised zone as well as free flow of medical evacuation from Srebrenica and the return of people to Srebrenica for family reunification. By virtue of your position, did you prepare this meeting or participate in it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall this meeting precisely, and I was in attendance, and I negotiated as part of a team on the Serb side. It was chaired by DutchBat commander, and it was held in DutchBat -- in the DutchBat base in Potocari. There were representatives of both the Muslim and Serb side. On the Serb side, there was a military team. And on the Muslim side, there was a mixed team; in other words, Naser Oric with his chief of security, and the representatives of the civilian authorities. The meeting was actually chaired by Mr. Franken, who I believe was deputy commander of DutchBat, as well as Mr. Boering, I believe. I think the meeting was attended by a military observer representative as well. We discussed all these matters, whereas the main point was to establish the line of -- lines of demilitarisation around Srebrenica as it remained undefined. The Drina Corps command and the Main Staff kept insisting on the need to solve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although the agreement had a precise map, but it seems there was some confusion in the field or that people simply did not honour the agreement in terms of the map. Was this your experience?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to see what the agreed borders of the enclave were. On the map it slightly differed -- or, rather, not slightly, but it differed from the situation in the field. Irrespective of the set borders, we remained at our lines. We tried to rely on the features that are there, such as hills, elevations, river beds, streams, valleys, so that both in reality and on the map we tried to reconcile the borders of the enclave. We did deviate from the agreement in such parts of territory where one cannot see anything, because of the location of the border. If there was a depression, we moved to the next vantage point, and that is where the Serb forces took up their positions and dug out trenches. The thing that was disputed the most was in the area of Zeleni Jadar, and we were never able to come to terms about that, whereas the rest of the borders were agreed and harmonised with the map as well as in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it mean that you gave in sometimes and left a valley to them by choosing the next vantage point, which may not have been necessarily in the enclave but outside? In other words, sometimes your movements were to their benefit?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were concessions on both sides. I need to say for the sake of the Chamber that one doesn't need to be physically present in order to control an area. You can control it from your firing positions 4- or 5- or 600 metres away. We knew where the borders were. But since we wanted to have a better tactical position and a safer situation for our troops, we did make certain concessions as did the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At this meeting it was more or less agreed that lists of the sick and students be created and cases of family reunification, and it seems that the Serb side accepted everything. It only requested that the Serbs who were still in Srebrenica be allowed to leave freely. There is the sentence: An agreement was reached that lists be drafted by the 30th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you exactly what this is about. There were frequent requests from the enclave to transport and evacuate the wounded, seriously wounded, and sick. In other words, those who could not be provided adequate medical treatment in the enclave or in the medical institutions in Srebrenica.
