That's why we agreed that all those they wanted to have evacuated to Tuzla, Sarajevo, or Kladanj should be put on a list which was supposed to be forwarded to me, and then I was to send that list with an explanation to my superior command, because they were responsible for issuing a permit or refusing a permit. I also requested in turn, since there were still Serbs in the enclave, mostly the elderly, I simply wanted to know for certain whether they wanted to leave Srebrenica or not. I knew what the situation was like, and I knew it was difficult to remain. That is why I asked them to bring those people physically to see them at the Yellow Bridge and to ask them myself whether they wanted to leave Srebrenica or not. Indeed, it developed that way. They brought everyone who was still in Srebrenica to the bridge, and when the people wanted to go, we organised their departure. There were, however, one or two women who did not want to abandon their apartments or houses and they remained. That's it regarding the issue of departures. Did you ask me about anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To put it briefly, is it correct that both you and your superior commands were very forthcoming and that when it came to the sick and students, you approved their requests basically always without imposing any restrictions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any individual request on their part was sent by me to the Drina Corps command. In most of the cases, there were no problems about evacuating the sick to Tuzla. I knew some of the people who were evacuated personally. Some of them had been injured or had spinal injuries, et cetera. So there was no problem in that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we even allowed political figures to go to Sarajevo if they were to attend peace talks? We even provided approvals for their departure, and you probably controlled that aspect of the situation in terms of their representatives leaving.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, and I think I still remember the fact that there were no departures across the Yellow Bridge. I don't think there were any requests in that regard. Maybe there were some direct requests put to the senior commands, but as far as I recall, not a single such request came to me. In other words, their political or military representatives did not go across the Yellow Bridge as far as I remember. I did not receive such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you had no control of them being put on board of a helicopter? It happened in Sokolac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We couldn't control that. We didn't know who was transported to Sarajevo by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be marked for identification, and the translation has perhaps already arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2066, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct if I say that in that respect, the Serbian side showed that it took into consideration humanitarian civilian issues that concerned the population in Srebrenica? Even the students were allowed to leave, as we can see in this document relating to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that with regard to all the issues that we discussed and reached an agreement on, the Serbian side respected the agreement. The obligations undertaken were respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the course of the examination-in-chief, you mentioned convoys, and the Chamber asked you about UNPROFOR convoys. Do you agree that the convoys were quite frequent and that many convoys entered the area, a far greater number of convoys entered the area than said in the media?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll first answer the last part of your question. I can't say how this was presented in the media or what actually entered the area. I didn't follow this, but what I can confirm is that the convoys did enter the area in accordance with the requests and the plans and the authorisation provided by our authorities, the organs who were responsible for such issues. Sometimes there were frequent convoys, numerous entries. Sometimes it wasn't that frequent. But they had their own plans, and having obtained authorisation, they would go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct if I say that you had fewer irregularities reported because these irregularities would be detected at the entrance to Republika Srpska? So you had fewer problems, fewer actions to take than those who were at Karakaj. You didn't have to prohibit entry as much as they did, or restrict entry as much as they did.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the experience they had in Karakaj or at other check-points. All I can talk about is the Yellow Bridge check-point where the military police was engaged, and I was occasionally present there, too, as well as organs from my brigade. So I can tell you about that check-point and back up what I say with arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to have a look at -- could we have a look at 65 ter 3688.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this one such authorisation, dated the 29th of April, 1995? Authorisation provided for a convoy. It says what it consists of, technical assistance, an ambulance, three lorries with trailers. And there's a convoy for Srebrenica, personal equipment. Is this the usual sort of pass for entry, dated the 29th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a customary authorisation provided for a convoy that entered or had to leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2067, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at 65 ter document 3689.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this document. Is it the 30th of April, one day later? So we have one for Karakaj, then two for Karakaj, two lorries, and three for Karakaj, two 18-tonne lorries, and then other things. The first one is for Gorazde, flour, nine lorries of flour, 28 tonnes, and beans, and so on and so forth. Is that the customary pass issued by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that's a day after the previous one we saw; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2068, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at 65 ter document 3691.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the date here is the 12th of May here and there is flour for Gorazde and for Srebrenica as well as beans. Then it says Karakaj, Drinjaca, and then for Srebrenica Russian flour, 16 tonnes, then the Swedish thing, the Swedish project. This was authorised on the 12th of May; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2069, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 65 ter document 3690.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date here is the 9th of May, 1995. Authorisation is given to grant the request for a certain body for humanitarian -- from a certain body for humanitarian aid. It says on the Zvornik-Bratunac-Srebrenica axis and then back, an ICRC team will travel along that road. Then you have the names of the people who will be on the team. Plastics are being provided, and so on and so forth. Do you know about this? It's the usual form of authorisation provided for the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these authorisations that concern entry into Srebrenica arrived in my brigade. I can't remember each and every authorisation, but this is the usual way in which such authorisation was provided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2070, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 3692 now, which is also a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The date here is the 16th of May. Is this also a convoy, an UNPROFOR convoy, a Dutch-Belgian convoy from Kiseljak to Srebrenica? So they came from other directions as well, not only from Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were supplies or convoys that arrived from various directions, not only from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2071, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at 65 ter document 3693. The 17th of May, 1995. On that date, again, the coordinating body made a request and authorisation was provided by the Main Staff which was sent to the Drina Corps command. Let's have a look at item 1, delivery of medical supplies, construction material, hygiene supplies for an MSF team in Srebrenica, and this was to be done on the 18th. And then the route is mentioned that is to be used. Further down, all these needs which were authorised are listed. Then under item 2, that also concerns Srebrenica, from Belgrade via Zvornik. Then item 3, the return of some of those convoys is mentioned. Could we have a look at the third page. I think there's nothing on the second one in the Serbian. It says that this passage was approved by the weekly plan of the UNHCR whose implementation was in course. It said check things and make the passage possible along the route mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the usual way of providing authorisation for such convoys?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2072, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 65 ter document 3694.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is authorisation provided? Again it's a request from the coordinating body, Republika Srpska, and it has to do with the delivery of UNHCR humanitarian aid. And then it says the 25th, Kotorman, Gorazde, and then Karakaj, Srebrenica. On the 21st of May, Kotorman, Gorazde, Karakaj, Srebrenica. It mentions beans, flour. And then it mentions flour and 9 tonnes of beans, 39 tonnes of flour. And then on the 24th of May, Karakaj, Srebrenica, 2 tonnes of beans and other items. Sugar, 17 and a half tonnes of sugar, and so on. Then Karakaj, Zepa, Karakaj, Gorazde. Here we have the 25th of May. That is a mistake. The 25th of April. Do you agree? Well, in fact, can we see the third page in the Serbian? Then there's something for Srebrenica and Mladenovac -- no, this in fact concerns the return. Gorazde, Rajkovac, Srebrenica, Mladenovac, Mladenovici, UNHCR. And then the 24th of May, you have the names of some people who were provided with authorisation. So there's quite a lot of traffic to Srebrenica. Wouldn't you say so, Mr. Nikolic? Quite a few things were authorised here and quite a few things were delivered.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't comment on that. As for authorisation provided, all those things went in. I think this was a weekly supply. There were daily supplies provided, and there were authorisations provided for weekly entries of those convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When such authorisation is provided, no one prevented anyone from entering at the Yellow Bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just be precise. This authorisation was issued in written form unless subsequently an oral order was passed down the chain of command. Then the Main Staff of the Drina Corps and the Bratunac Brigade might issue an order and then everything would enter. There were exceptions when an oral order would subsequently be issued and that concerned restricting the entry of certain supplies. They were there in April, May, and June, in that period of time. So if there were no such interventions, if there were no subsequent requests, then this authorisation was binding for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sometimes between the time that passed between the authorisation and the entry of the convoy there was combat, and this would be a genuine reason, a good reason for which a convoy would have to wait to enter the area. I'm not just talking about the year 1995. I'm talking about the period as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the entry of convoys being postponed because of active combat that was still ongoing. If there were such cases, if there was such combat it couldn't really influence the passage of convoys because the routes used by the convoys were quite safe. On the whole, when there were incidents it was in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. You are only speaking about your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only about my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2073, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at 65 ter document 3695.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this. It's the 22nd of May, 1995, and it says there what it was that was approved. This mainly has to do with Sarajevo. Let us see what pertains to your zone. Do you see the second paragraph? "We have not approved the transport of containers with oils, grease, solvents, and antifreeze." This seems to be industrial products rather than anything else; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with what is written here. That is the only part that I agree with. As for the rest, I don't know what types of oil these were, and I cannot comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at page 3 now -- or, actually, page 2, but it's the third one as well for some ... You can see further on what else was approved. And then can we go one page up to see what it was that they did not approve. In Serbian, we see the lower half, and it says: "We would also like to inform you that we have not approved the transport of the following convoys and teams: Diesel" -- something for the canteen. Then 4, some kind of rotation of personnel. Then gas, oil, rotation of personnel. Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that all of this has to do primarily with restricting -- or, rather, imposing restrictions upon UNPROFOR rather than the population? Gasoline, diesel. Number 16. It says from Srebrenica to Koviljaca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "19. Transporting a new team of civilian police from Sarajevo to Srebrenica." Do you agree that most of this has to do with the military, military materiel, things that can be used as military materiel? Does most of this not apply to that rather than food for the population?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree with that. I did not really focus on the first page if this convoy -- or, rather, if this approval is for the Dutch Battalion and UNPROFOR forces, then I absolutely agree that everything that is being brought in is intended for the Dutch Battalion, not civilians. So then there is the military observers, and there is civilian police, and that certainly differs from the humanitarian convoys that were approved by the UNHCR and that went through them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2074, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 65 ter 3697.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that this is the 26th of May? This seems to be a weekly document as the one from the 20th of May. We agree for the weekly plan of humanitarian aid supplies to be observed from the 27th of May until the 1st of June, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is customary, isn't it, as far as weekly plans go?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is signed by General Manojlo Milovanovic, Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2075, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 3698?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is more here, isn't that right? It includes Russian convoys as well. Is this the 26th of May? And then there is Karakaj and Srebrenica here, the Russian convoy, and then Karakaj, Srebrenica. There is Kotorman, Gorazde, and Karakaj, Srebrenica for the 27th and the 28th of May. Then the 30th of May, Karakaj, Srebrenica, Russian. I don't know how many -- 64 metric tonnes of flour. And then further down Karakaj, Srebrenica, 5 tonnes of something. I don't know what. Then the 31st of May, Russian. I don't know how many tonnes of flour, 2.1 tonnes of beans, 1.376 boxes of beef, 18 boxes of dummies, one -- for babies that is. One lorry of school equipment. Can we move on to page 3 now. There's something written here. Can you recognise the handwriting? Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know whose it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here: "As already stated, my battalion still has a mission to guard the population in the safe area." Right? And then there's some reference to making life difficult for observers on the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is all about, and I have no comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the last page. The next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we see here what the restriction refers to. We agree that on Wednesday, the 30th of May, 1995, a satellite telex should be brought to Srebrenica along with equipment that is necessary for the UNHCR office. So the army has this suspicion here that this could jeopardise their security, this telex. Do you agree that that is exclusively in the hands of the army itself, that it's not for the civilian authorities to say, and that approvals or lack of approval is guided by their feeling of security regarding these things for which approval is sought?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't really want to comment on this conclusion of yours. It is well known who is supposed to take care of the security of units and staffs. That is clearly defined, and I would have no special comment in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I know that some of the members of the Trial Chamber are familiar with military matters, but who is in charge of security? Can the co-ordination body order something to the Main Staff that would work to the detriment of the security of the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very clear answer there. First of all, I cannot even imagine any such thing, that someone from the co-ordination body, where serious and responsible people are, I cannot imagine them doing anything that would jeopardise the security of the army that they belonged to. Whose army is this? If I know that Vice-President Koljevic sat on this co-ordination body and Biljana Plavsic for a while, and Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic, I certainly cannot assume that they would make any decision that would be against the interests of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber whether it is correct that the question of the security of the army itself is exclusively under the army, that it does have the right to protect itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I mean, maybe Mr. Karadzic can break it down a bit, because the question is whether it is correct that the question of the security of the army itself is exclusively under the army. I don't know what that means. It's so broad. If you're talking about who has the power or right to say that a certain piece of equipment goes on a convoy into an enclave, that's one thing, but the way it's phrased I think is so overly broad as to be not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. Nicholls. Could you reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that it is the duty of the army to take care of this, to see whether something that is brought through the lines would work to their detriment? Are they supposed to assess that, and are they supposed to take protective measures that would protect them from that kind of damage?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I fully understood your first question as well. Security and taking preventive security measures, that is to say, to prevent any kind of misunderstanding and any kind of jeopardy with regard to the units themselves, is exclusively under the jurisdiction of military organs. The next thing I wish to say is that at the same time this is indeed under the military, but it is also in the interest of the political leadership not to jeopardise the security interests of soldiers and of the army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2076, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, wasn't the last one 76? 26th of May. This is the 28th of May. Or maybe I didn't even tender it. The 26th of May, can that be tendered as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What it's 65 ter number, Mr. Karadzic? I don't think you tendered it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3698.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's what we just admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I probably haven't called up this one yet, 3699 then. Could that please be called up, 65 ter number 3699.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to focus on this, the 28th of May. Approval is given for Srebrenica from Skelani, Bijeljina, et cetera, 30th of May, 1995, arrival, departure. The name of the team leader is provided, and then 2 tonnes of cement and 200 litres of diesel, et cetera. That is for Srebrenica. Is that the usual form of such approvals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a look at the next page. It's hard for me to read somebody else's handwriting. There is some note here. Somebody is writing to Colonel Vukovic and saying the road they wish to use via Zeleni Jadar is within the boundaries of the safe area of Srebrenica. "I cannot grant your request."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So did the route sometimes have to be changed for some reason?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what I see before me, in this particular case I really don't know what this is all about, and I wouldn't want to speculate. However, often there were requests to change the route to Srebrenica. When arriving from Zvornik along the Drina, Zvornik, Drinjaca, Zeleni Polom, Kasin Polje [phoen], Drinski Most, Bratunac, Srebrenica, that was the route, and there were often requests made for the convoy to take the asphalt road, because the road that they had received permission to use was a macadam road. So that is the only thing I can say in relation to the question that you put to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that this is a draft translation. Whose translation is this, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly of the team. I'm not sure. Oh, OTP, it's theirs, because we don't have this seal or stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe it is a CLSS translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking because I didn't see any translation of the handwritten part. Probably most of them were noted as illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe if we go to the last page, I don't have it up on my screen anymore, that it does make a reference to the last ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see only "Illegible," and then there's no note -- referring to the handwritten part. Whether it makes sense or not, Mr. Nikolic, could you read this part? Is it legible to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try. I shall try. I cannot. I just see until the beginning: "In view of your request, that" -- I cannot. I cannot discern this. I really cannot decipher this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Given -- I note the time. We will take a break now for an hour and resume at 1.30. The last one we haven't given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2077, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have 1D5106. It seems that we still have no translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 3rd of January, 1995, Colonel Palic said that he was to transport some assets between Zepa and Srebrenica, and that out of the five received RPG-7s, he should be allowed to have four instead of two that were planned. Is it an anti-armour asset?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. RPG-7, as we can see, is a launcher used to launch missiles or shells aimed at destroying armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2078, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I was informed by the court officer as to the potential misunderstanding about the -- about the amount of time for your cross-examination. The Chamber clearly stated that you should not exceed the time, the same amount of time, which is spent by the Prosecution, which is 6 hours and 15 minutes. I think you have spend so far four hours and 20 minutes. You will have a bit less than two hours exactly. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I state my position on this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I planned my cross-examination based on the previously announced nine hours asked by the Prosecution. On the other hand, we also wanted Mr. Tucker's testimony pertaining to 1993 to be excluded, which was not accepted by the Bench. In other words, I have an intelligence officer here who is very familiar with 1993. It would be a shame to gain first-hand knowledge from the -- this intelligence officer. That is why I focused on 1993 so much, because other than this witness, I have no other Prosecution witnesses to examine on that topic. Therefore, I had planned to use nine hours, and I wanted to ask you to be allowed to continue throughout the day tomorrow, because my assessment was based on the previous OTP assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Apart from the issue of our understanding of the -- what the Chamber communicated, which I think was clear, the fact is that most of Dr. Karadzic's time has been spent with eliciting evidence favourable to his case that was not touched upon by the cross-examination is something that the Chamber wouldn't have known before when it made its ruling that he was to have the same amount of time as the Prosecutor. So I would ask you to consider, having now heard the cross-examination, that it was necessary for him to cover topics that are eliciting evidence favourable to our defence case, and so the time should not be the same. We should be given some additional time to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I make any comment myself, I will consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will rise to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm so sorry, I know the Court is trying to get away, but it occurred to me that I might have some quick scheduling information that the Court would maybe not want to hear about after it had deliberated and it may be significant to it. So there were two quick matters that perhaps should be raised. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. We'll hear you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, as you know, the OTP has been quite successful thus far in accommodating shifts from normal sittings to extended sittings without any gaps and that was through, as I've mentioned before, some very extensive and even heroic efforts by people behind the scenes. In this instance, we are clearly having difficulty in filling the added time resulting from the extended sittings for next week, and I was, in any event, going to alert the Court to the prospect that we would have a gap by virtue of the additional time from the extended sittings next week. Secondly, I know that Mr. Robinson has raised the issue of Mr. Block's testimony, and I just -- the Court -- I don't know the extent to which the Court is familiar with that. I can discuss that now if necessary, but if the Court's already aware of that possibility in calculating or in assessing whatever impact the schedule over the next few days may have on its decision in this instance, then I don't need to raise it, but I will say I have had some discussions with Mr. Robinson about it. While I don't agree with all of the factors he raised, I also indicated to him that the OTP did not have any objection to Mr. Block proceeding on Tuesday and, in fact, considered that -- considered that we agreed with that as an appropriate schedule. So I thought it best to let the Court know now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just to have a full option, how long do you expect that Mr. Block's evidence in chief will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think an hour or less, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His amalgamated statement contains how many pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thirteen. If led live, how long would that take? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour to stand up with -- the two of us, but I'm familiar with that statement. I think it will be, as Mr. Tieger said, less than an hour. That's the outside --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if led live.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. If led live, I think it would be on the order of about two hours. And I think not live, it would be less than an hour by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- by quite some measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise for 15 minutes. --- Break taken at 1.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber observes that there is no absolute right for the accused to be granted the same amount of time for cross-examination as used by the Prosecution. As a matter of fact, the Chamber was originally of the view that the accused could adequately cross-examine this witness in four to four and a half hours. However, in the circumstances, the Chamber considered that it would be appropriate to allow the accused, as a maximum, to use the same amount of time as used by the Prosecution for their direct examination. However, the Chamber takes into account the accused's argument that there was a misunderstanding, and given this, the Chamber exercises its discretion and allows you to complete your cross-examination within three and a half hours from now. That will make in total about eight hours. However, the Chamber will exercise stricter control over the direction of this cross-examination and urges you to start with and concentrate on core issues of this case. And I emphasise again you need to prioritise your lines of questions. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you very much. [Interpretation] Could we see 1D5101.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for that, let me ask you the following: Did you know that the Muslim side was planning and, in fact, commenced, as of the 15th of May and the 15th of June, large-scale operations throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the Zepa area. The purpose was to assist the forces around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I had information of a general kind, nothing very specific, and all I want to say is that I know nothing about those matters and don't want to testify about them. If there's anything that concerns Srebrenica and my brigade's area of responsibility, that is acceptable, but given the issues that you have just mentioned, well, I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree - this is something you must have noticed - that the 28th Division and the 8th Operations Group as of the 15th of June stepped up its combat activities in the Srebrenica area. And here we have seen documents in which they say that this is what they were doing in order to help Sarajevo. Did you hear this increased level of combat activities as of the 15th of June?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're speaking about 1995, I assume, June 1995. I can tell you that I regularly and intensively assessed the intentions of the 28th Division, of the 28th Division's forces, and I had fairly reliable information about their intentions. And naturally I knew about the incidents that occurred during that period of time. In my area of responsibility, I was aware of all the incidents. After so much time has passed I can't remember all of those incidents, but I know that there were sniper incidents. The enclave would be left, ambushes would be laid, and so on and so forth. There was such activity during that period of time that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Without going into the details, can we base ourselves on your awareness of their intentions? Is it correct that their intention was to extend the so-called free area, to link it up with Kladanj and Tuzla, and to drive out the Serbian troops and the Serbs from Podrinje?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my assessments, I, on the whole, always attempted to establish what their intentions were, what the intentions of the forces from Srebrenica were, to establish what their final objective was. There's a series of activities that pointed to their intentions. That included Oric's departure, with trips to Tuzla and supplies and increased communications between Zepa and Srebrenica. And on the basis of the overall situation and all the intelligence that I had, I made an assessment which I forwarded to the Drina Corps command, and in that report I drew the following conclusions. The 28th Division had the following intention: In the forthcoming period, they wanted to act together with forces and a unit from Zepa, the forces of the 8th Operations Group, and at one point in time they wanted to break out at the Zepa, Han Pijesak, Pjenavac, Kladanj, Crni Vrh, Tuzla axis, and from that position they wanted to launch an offensive, the purpose of which would be to clear that area, and that included Podrinje. They wanted to feed the Serbian forces in that area, in fact. So in general terms that was my assessment of their objective at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You reported to the corps command and what you knew of was probably something that the Main Staff also knew. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost convinced of the fact. I can't really confirm that, but since I know how reporting proceeds and how you forward intelligence and intelligence assessments, well, naturally the corps command received that information, because the report was addressed to them, but I'm sure that all that information, all these important assessments, all these intelligence assessments reached the top of the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at the following: The VRS Main Staff knew what their plans were, and could you have a look at what was authorised at the time. This is a document from the UNHCR. So what was authorised for Srebrenica? Look at it, on the 27th of June, 1995, 8.5, 12.5 tonnes of sugar. Then you've got oil, 7.5 tonnes, then 6 tonnes of beans, 7 tonnes, and 300 -- 3 tonnes of a different kind of beans. That's the 27th of June, and it was just prior to the Srebrenica operation. Fifty-three tonnes of food for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says here in this document. I didn't see the title. Is it an authorisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A report according to which this was authorised. Could we have a look at the next page. This is for the 27th of June. It's a report on the leader of the team -- or from the leader of the team to people who entered the area. So if you receive such information or such a document, they go in. Your people let them through. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've explained the procedure on a number of occasions when you showed similar authorisations to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, are you in a position to explain to us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This document is a list from the Russian humanitarian convoy for Srebrenica. The date is the 27th of June, 1995. We have the personal details that concern the convoy, the leader, the driver, and then there's the notification number, other information. It's a humanitarian convoy for the Srebrenica enclave. That's what I can see. Those are the conclusions I can draw when I have a cursory look at the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the last numbers are notification numbers. Did you say so? IMP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think these are the identification numbers on the cards that they have on them. That's what I know from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So does it mean that they entered Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Yes. I can't confirm that on the basis of this document because I don't see that it says that they entered Srebrenica anywhere. What I can see is that it's a list from the Russian humanitarian convoy for Srebrenica. Then I see the date 27th of June, 1995. However, it is customary to have in addition to these names, in addition to the drivers, there's a list of the lorries, of the vehicles used. They are specified. The registration number is specified. The type of car and the quantity and kind of goods that is being delivered is also mentioned. I can't see this in this document. I can't comment on that, because on the basis of this document I can't see how many lorries are entering. I can't see what is entering Srebrenica and what quantities are at stake. All I can see is that drivers are mentioned. We have some names, it mentions UNHCR members, and as far as I can understand the document, these numbers here are the numbers that they have on their identification cards. Those are the conclusions I can draw from these documents if I go into a detailed analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance in this document -- well, the document consists of a number of pages. If we go through it, we'll reach other pages. In the previous one, it's the 27th of June, and there's equipment. Here we have individuals who are mentioned. Can we go through it? Can we see the other pages? Here it's the 20th of June, 1995. That's the date, and it says that they entered -- these ticks here mean that they entered the area. Isn't that correct? And the number 34 was corrected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Karadzic? On what basis does Mr. Nikolic know this? How can he know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, is this how you would mark the documents when someone entered the area? Would this mean that someone entered the area?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this kind of document, the one I have in front of me, now that 17 years have passed, I cannot reliably tell you whether they entered or not. I can't tell you about that, the fact that someone used a pen or a felt-tip to tick these markings off doesn't show that they entered Srebrenica, for me. I will be even more precise. What I can see here is something that could have taken place at the first check-point at Karakaj. This could have been done there, or in Sarajevo, at the pass. This could have been done anywhere else. Someone could have taken a pen and made these markings at these other places. So the only conclusion that one can draw is that this document is a document that someone who is responsible for controls had on him. He carried out certain controls, but nothing else can be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's go through the remainder of the document. Everything is there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's see the remainder of the document. Could we see the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is for the 20th of June. It has to do with quantities expressed in tonnes. We have soap, sugar, beans, canned fish, powdered milk, biscuits, flour, canned fish, et cetera, et cetera. Does it say 55 tonnes?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in order to be sure that I've understood you -- I see the date here, the 20th of June, 1995. Before that, I saw that the driver had the date of the 27th, if I remember correctly. Can you explain this to me? Can you tell me whether the goods that I see registered here under this date -- or, rather, the drivers, were those the drivers who were driving this cargo, and were they on that list of the 27th? That is what creates confusion as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll see, Mr. Nikolic, but the convoy that goes on a particular day, for example, this truck, 657, is carrying 4 tonnes of soap. The other one also has 4 tonnes of soap. Then this other one has 8 tonnes of sugar, and so on. Now we are going to see what the grand total is in the report of Republika Srpska. So we're going to see the quantities that are entering the area at the time of this large-scale Muslim offensive against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple points, Your Honour. One, unfortunately we don't have a translation of any of these, it appears, so I can't tell exactly what they say, but Mr. Karadzic, at page 68, around line 8, started all these authorisations, which I don't think he's established other than saying they are in any way and wasn't able to do through the witness. Second, if it saves any time to remind him our case is not that no convoys ever entered Srebrenica. Our case is clearly spelled out, and I won't refer to the document, but there -- in our view, there was to be an unobtrusive reduction, which was not to garner bad publicity but at the same time to create poor conditions in the enclave. So the fact that showing each individual particular convoy that went through -- it's not up to me to say where he's going, but it's not our case that no convoys went through at any time, which appears to be what he's combatting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, I'm wondering whether this witness is an appropriate one to deal with these global convoy issues. Mr. Karadzic, I told you to come to the core issues of the case, in particular the issues raised in his examination-in-chief, but still you are insisting upon this line of question. The Chamber is not interfering with your line of questioning or conduct of your cross-examination, but bear that in mind. Your time is limited.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. However, I kindly ask that we move on. First of all, the most dangerous accusation is contained in the following: That for political or military reasons we were denying people food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic, it is not time for your submission. Ask questions to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we have page 313 of this -- of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, let me ask you, when leaving Republika Srpska and when entering Srebrenica, did your service check convoys?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Convoys were checked in detail when they would leave the enclave of Srebrenica going to Zagreb, Belgrade, wherever they went. That was our obligation on the basis of the order that we had received from the corps command and the Main Staff. Other check-points checked them when they were entering Karakaj from Serbia and elsewhere, when they were entering the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So at the bridge, you only conducted these superficial checks or you did not check at all whatever had been checked previously at Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did check all the convoys that were entering. Sometimes it wasn't a detailed check, but sometimes when there were reinforced measures of control, then these checks were detailed, although there had been checks in Karakaj, although the police would escort them to the Yellow Bridge. In this period that I have already mentioned, March, April, May, June, the beginning of the operation, we had conducted intensive checks of these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get page 3 of this. We're going to skip individual days, so three pages further ahead. 308 is the last ERN number. One page further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is the State Committee for Cooperation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations co-ordination body for humanitarian operations, and do you agree that the date is the 22nd of June, and that it says from the 21st of June until the 30th of June, the following has been approved, and so on and so forth? Is that right? This is a weekly approval; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm what is written here. I cannot confirm anything beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page is empty, so can we have the one after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Underneath the UNHCR sign, is that a stamp of Republika Srpska, "Co-ordination body for humanitarian aid," the 22nd of June, 1995, and then it is specified what it was that was approved. And further down there is the seal of Republika Srpska. You can see that at the bottom of the page. Karakaj, Srebrenica, the 27th of June, what we looked at a moment ago, and up there it's the 24th of June. And then can we have the next page now. The 23rd of June, Srebrenica, the Russian convoy. We've seen that specification. Then the 24th from Srebrenica, the names of persons who are drivers. And then the 27th of June. And further on, if we look at the next page, we will see that it goes all the way to the 30th. Is it correct, Mr. Nikolic, that at that time, this is basically until the end of June, that these convoys did pass through as had been approved by the co-ordination body? Did you stop them from getting through, or did they actually manage to get to their destination?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just feel it is necessary to say what really happened there, and that is the following: These separate permits that you presented to me, I mean, drivers on one list, cargos on the other list, I did not receive that in my brigade. And I don't know what it was like at this top level, at the level of the co-ordination body, how they communicated amongst themselves and how they reached agreement and how they came to final solutions. As for yellow -- as for the Yellow Bridge, as for my brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, we would get a permit where it said which is this convoy that has been approved when this entry has been allowed, for when, rather, and then there is a specific list of the content of the truck. So this is a complete document, including their -- the personnel bringing in these goods, the numbers of their IDs, and the cargos that are being brought in. That is the kind of complete document that I would receive. So now you've created a bit of confusion in my mind. That is the kind of document that I used to see, whereas what you've shown me is how this happens gradually, how this final approval is created, if you will. So what we used to receive was what I told you about a moment ago. Once we received all of that, then we have all this information from that approval and we see what it is that is supposed to enter, and then we act in accordance with orders. I have already told you, for us, it was this approval that was binding except in situations when in addition to a written approval, we do not get oral orders stating that we should look more carefully or why we should say, Wait a moment. You cannot enter yet. And then they would wait. So this was the general course of action that was taken for all who entered Srebrenica or left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Cyrillic we see what it says at the top of the page and we also see the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tried to be very patient, but this is another example of wasting your time, Mr. Karadzic. All the witness can do is confirm what is written in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page of the document so that it is clearer. I am asking the witness the following: This shows that it has been approved, and I'm asking whether anyone stopped that from happening at the Yellow Bridge, or was all of this that has been approved actually brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You heard the submission of Mr. Nicholls. He can repeat. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to make an objection, Your Honour. That's a question that has been asked and answered over and over again, where the witness stated, We followed the approvals we received from the Main Staff through the Drina Corps to my brigade, and we followed them unless we received an oral order to the contrary. So the question has been answered more than once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nicholls, I take it that General Milovanovic is coming as your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who is the author of the clearance documents we saw earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very, very many of them bear his signature, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I told you many times to prioritise your questions, and even allowing you some extension, I told you to come to the issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. All right. If General Milovanovic is really going to come, but I have no assurance to the effect that they might give up on this altogether as they have done before, so I was afraid that this would be my last opportunity. But let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, do you know, do you agree that at that point in time, say, on the 4th and on the 7th of July, 1995, large groups left Srebrenica to reconnoiter and to carry out terrorist operations against our population and that they even charted the course that they would take during their withdrawal on the 11th and 12th? Were you aware of these departures of theirs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th and 7th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are in 1995 now throughout.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any exits on the 4th or 7th of July, because the operation started on the 6th, and absolutely this is the first time that I hear this kind of information, that they got out on the 4th and 7th of July and carried out various actions, operations. This is the first time I hear this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe this document has already been admitted on some occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5083. Can we zoom in for the benefit of the witness. I don't know if the translation is done. I'm expecting an answer from Ram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyway, do you agree that this is a document dated the 4th of July, 1995, and it's a report sent to the command of the 283rd Light East Bosnian Brigade. Just take a look at what they did and where they were. The task of the group was to secure the road between Jelenca, Ljeskovik, and so on and so forth, and two other groups continued moving along Bijela Voda, Ljeskovik, and so on. Could you please take a look at this. And it says there were 32 soldiers in one group and there were 18 soldiers from their group. They rested for two hours and then went towards Zeleni Jadar. They killed some men on an APC. I think that you confirmed that earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this report, and really, now, I mean, you've given me a countless amount of information. I really should take a proper look at this. I mean, let me just take a look. This is a report of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 283rd Brigade. I don't know, really. Really. I don't know about these events. I don't know. I have never heard of these activities specifically, especially not the 7th of July, 1995. And they refer to Ljeskovik and these other villages. In order to get to Ljeskovik, they have to leave the enclave, and they have to go deep into territory that is not under their control -- or, rather, through territory that is not under their control. So believe me, I don't know. I cannot give any comment with regard to this report because this is the first time I see it, and I'm unaware of all of these things having happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Memiseva Vodenica [phoen], and do you know that that is when they killed some of our men in an ambush? Take a look at this: "When we arrived at Sinan's house near Osmace, a TAM van came. They killed some people, stole some things." Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about their sabotage activities and an ambush they laid for a lorry, but this was a police lorry. There were 10 or 11 policemen involved, I believe, but that incident did not occur on this date. I heard about that incident, but not that it occurred on the date that you're referring to. That's my problem. The incident itself is not problematic for me. The problem is that I can't relate this to the report that you are showing me and to the date the 7th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 4th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't make any difference whether it's the 4th or the 7th. I can't make such a link.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, one, the witness has made it clear he can't comment on the document. Two, I can't read it, but if the document says some Muslim soldiers killed somebody and stole some things, what's the relevance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Before that, Mr. Nikolic, does this document refer to event on 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 4th of July, Your Honour. I don't know whom you put the question, Your Honour. It's the 4th of July. It was an action taken just before our action. And four soldiers were killed here, not 11 policemen. We had 11 policemen earlier on. It's the 4th of July, and four soldiers were killed in a van in the depth of our territory. The witness said this himself. If that's where they were, that was in the depth of our territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can tell you for certain, and I'm sure about this, is that the soldiers who were killed weren't killed in the area of responsibility of my brigade. That's what I know for certain. And if soldiers were killed, they weren't from my brigade, because I know for certain that during that period of time there were no soldiers killed from my brigade. If you show me the names of the individuals concerned, perhaps that would refresh my memory, but I doubt that I would forget such a thing, regardless of when it took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a Muslim document. There's no doubt about that. Isn't that correct? You can have a look at the last page to see the signature and the stamp. Do you know Seval Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no information about Seval. I don't know who this person is. This is the first time I've seen the document and his signature. I know who the Chief of Staff was, I know about him, but I know nothing about this man here. So whether this is a Muslim document or not, well, when I look at the stamp, I would say so, but I can't confirm whether this is an original document or not. That's not a question you can put to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you will not admit this document into evidence through this witness; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. Karadzic. We will not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After it's been uploaded, could we see the document dated the 7th of July, 1995, and a report from the command of the 28th Division to the 2nd Corps. This has to do about the reconnaissance they carried out along the line they would use to withdraw four days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just while we have a quiet moment, at the very end, Your Honours, I would like to make a very brief submission. It will only take a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's the case -- well, it will be uploaded tomorrow, and I hope the translation will also be available. In fact, it's been uploaded, but we're waiting for this to be officially done. If that is the situation, then we could give this time to Mr. Nicholls. Tomorrow we will be better equipped to examine this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nicholls, shall we excuse the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That's fine, Your Honour. I don't think it matters much, but that's fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. That would be fine, Your Honour. It won't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And would I ask to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right. Then I would like Mr. Nikolic to be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We continue tomorrow morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tomorrow, Mr. Karadzic, you will have two hours and 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Three hours -- I heard you the three hours and a half --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From then. So tomorrow you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I spent half an hour after you told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Forty-five minutes, Mr. Karadzic, 40 minutes. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
